title: Functions Checkpoint
intro: You can split a program into named pieces now: functions, prototypes, parameters, returns, references, overloads and scope. Thirteen rounds, one from every idea in this module. First-try answers earn three stars!

rounds.prompt: `main` calls `sayHello();`, but sayHello is defined below main and there is no prototype. What happens?
options: It works, because C++ reads the whole file before compiling
It compiles, but sayHello never runs
It runs sayHello after main finishes
A compile error: 'sayHello' was not declared in this scope
rounds.explain: The compiler reads from top to bottom. Define the function above main, or put a prototype such as `void sayHello();` above main.

rounds.prompt: In what order do these four lines appear?
rounds.explain: A call is a detour: C++ runs the whole function, then comes back to the line right after the call. Being written first in the file does not make step run first.

rounds.prompt: This line compiles, but the banner never appears. Why?
options: It needs the word void in front
The round brackets are missing, so the function is mentioned but not called
A function name cannot start with a lower-case letter
rounds.explain: A bare name is not a call. g++ at most warns about it, so the only clue is the missing output. The brackets are needed even when there is nothing to put in them.

rounds.prompt: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: An argument has a type, a parameter does not
They are two words for the same thing
The parameter is the slot declared in the function, the argument is the value passed in
Parameters are for numbers, arguments are for text
rounds.explain: `void printStars(int count)` declares the parameter. `printStars(7)` supplies the argument.
The function worked on a copy. Changing a plain parameter never touches the caller's variable: that is pass by value.

rounds.prompt: The only change from the last round is one character. What does this print now?
rounds.explain: `int& number` makes number another name for score, so adding ten to it changes main's variable. That is pass by reference.

rounds.prompt: What does this function hand back for grade(62)?
rounds.explain: The first `return` reached ends the function at once, so nothing below it runs. That is why early returns need no `else`.

rounds.prompt: This compiles, but category(75) produces garbage or crashes. Why?
options: string is not allowed as a return type
There are two returns in one function
An age of 60 or more reaches the end of the function with nothing returned
The chain needs a switch instead
rounds.explain: Every path through a non-void function must return a value. C++ builds it anyway and the result is undefined, so add a final `else` or a `return` after the chain.

rounds.prompt: What is the tidier way to write this?
options: It is already as short as it can be
rounds.explain: The comparison is already true or false, so it can be returned directly. Four lines become one.

rounds.prompt: Given `int half(int n)` and `double half(double n)`, both returning n / 2, what does this print?
rounds.code:
cout << half(9) << endl;
cout << half(9.0) << endl;
options: It does not compile: the call is ambiguous
rounds.explain: The type you write picks the overload. 9 is an int, so whole-number division chops the half off; 9.0 goes to the double version.

rounds.prompt: This function is called three times in a row. What does it print?
rounds.explain: A local variable is created fresh on every call and destroyed when the function ends, so it cannot remember anything between calls.

rounds.prompt: Match each piece of function vocabulary to what it means.

pairs.right: Hands nothing back to the caller
The first line of a function, ending in a semicolon
Hands a value back and ends the function
A parameter that is another name for the caller's variable
The region where a variable exists

rounds.explain: Six words that describe the whole module. Being able to name these makes every C++ error message easier to read.

rounds.prompt: Write a function that swaps the values of two of the caller's variables.
rounds.explain: Both parameters are references, so the swap reaches the caller's variables. `temp` holds a's value for a moment, because `a = b;` would otherwise wipe it out before it was saved.
